extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and appellate counsel handling IPRs (Federal Circuit appeals)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how the PTAB and Federal Circuit evaluate claim construction and obviousness in inter partes review appeals, including standards of review, burden of proof, evidentiary weighting, and procedural forfeiture. Useful for attorneys formulating IPR petitions, oppositions, and appellate briefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties' agreed-upon claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: When the parties have consistently advanced and litigated a particular claim construction before the Board, the Board may adopt that construction and evaluate the case accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a petitioner and respondent both treated claim terms as having a particular meaning (e.g., that the claim requires a server and a network switch box 'as separate and distinct components'), the Board may properly adopt that understanding. The record (petition, reply, expert testimony, hearing statements) showing consistent advocacy of the construction supports the Board's use of it on review. Example: Apple repeatedly characterized its theory as relying on Ahopelto's 'logically distinct' GGSN functions, so the Board adopted the parties' understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture of arguments not presented to the Board
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments or legal theories not presented to the PTAB are generally forfeited on appeal to the Federal Circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit will not consider arguments that were not raised before the Board because failing to present them 'deprives this court of the benefit of the Board’s informed judgment.' Authorities cited: Voice Tech Corp. v. Unified Pats., In re NuVasive. Practically, challengers must raise claim-construction or unworkability objections to the Board to preserve them for appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness standard of review (law/fact split)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness is a question of law based on underlying factual findings; the ultimate obviousness determination is reviewed de novo while underlying facts are reviewed for substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate courts review the Board's ultimate obviousness conclusion de novo and review factual findings (e.g., what the prior art discloses, motivation to combine, POSITA understanding) for substantial evidence. Cite: 'Obviousness is a question of law based on underlying facts.' and 'We review the Board’s ultimate determination of obviousness de novo and its underlying facts for substantial evidence.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial evidence standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Factual findings by the Board are upheld if supported by substantial evidence—i.e., if a reasonable factfinder could have reached the agency's conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantial evidence review asks 'whether a reasonable fact finder could have arrived at the agency’s decision.' If the record contains testimonial evidence, document disclosures, and expert opinions that support the Board's factual findings, the Federal Circuit will affirm. Citations: Intelligent Bio‑Sys., In re Gartside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-tiered approach to assessing prior-art disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating whether prior art discloses claimed elements, the Board may analyze (1) the prior-art disclosure itself, (2) testimonial (expert) evidence about how a POSITA would understand the disclosure, and (3) any additional cited references or evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board's review is not limited to verbatim claim term recitations or architecture diagrams; it sequentially examines the text of the reference, assesses expert testimony about the skilled artisan's understanding, and then considers other cited references to determine whether the claimed elements are shown as distinct components. Example: the Board found Ahopelto did not expressly describe 'a server' and a separate 'network switch box', then looked at testimony and additional evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden to show prior art discloses distinct claim elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The petitioner must prove that the prior art would have been understood by a POSITA to disclose the claimed elements, including any requirement that elements be 'separate and distinct' (whether logically or physically).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim requires separate and distinct components, petitioner must show the prior art teaches those components as separate/logically distinct entities. Merely pointing to different functions within an overarching process is insufficient unless the record supports that those functions would have been understood as distinct components. Example: petitioner failed to show Ahopelto’s GGSN included a server functionality separate from its routing functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of logical vs physical separateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may require elements to be 'logically separate and distinct' rather than physically separate; whether that construction is appropriate depends on the parties' positions and record evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party can consistently argue for logical separate-and-distinctness (e.g., different logical/software entities on a shared platform), and the Board can adopt that construction; the Board acknowledged that physical separation is not required. However, the petitioner still must show the prior art teaches the logical separation. If a party wishes to challenge the appropriateness of a logical-separation requirement (e.g., 'box-drawing' problem in software), that challenge must be presented to the Board to avoid forfeiture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight and credibility of expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board's credibility assessments of expert witnesses are entitled to deference, and the Board may give little weight to expert testimony that fails to point to supporting references or that concedes overlap with challenged disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit defers to the Board on expert credibility. If an expert cannot point to references showing the asserted distinction or admits overlap (e.g., that claimed functionality overlaps with an overarching process in the prior art), the Board may reasonably discount that testimony. Example: the Board gave 'little weight' to Dr. Jensen because he could not point to any reference showing implementation of server and routing functionality as different logical entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedded/multi-function prior-art disclosures may not satisfy separate-element claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If a prior-art reference describes multiple functions as part of an overarching process (rather than as separate modules or components), that reference may not satisfy claim elements requiring separate and distinct components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When prior art embeds multiple functions within a single routing procedure or process, the Board may reasonably find that it does not disclose separate claim elements. Example: Ahopelto's routing procedure encompassed both the 'server' and 'routing' functionalities, so the Board found it did not disclose them as separate components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to explain modification or combination with additional references
rubrics_metrics.description: When relying on additional references to alter the understanding of a primary reference, a petitioner must argue and show how a skilled artisan would have modified the primary reference with those teachings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board expects the petitioner to articulate and support a theory of modification or combination: simply citing additional references without arguing how they would modify the primary prior art is insufficient. In the case, Apple did not argue that a skilled artisan would have modified Ahopelto with the additional references, so the Board found those citations did not alter its conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate reliance on the full record to evaluate Board findings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit will consider the full administrative record (petitions, replies, expert declarations, hearing statements) when assessing whether the Board's factual findings and claim constructions were proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements and positions across the record (petition text, reply briefs, expert testimony, hearing responses) can bind parties' positions and justify the Board's chosen construction or assessment. Example: Apple's repeated descriptions in the petition/reply/hearing that its theory relied on 'logically distinct' GGSN functions supported the Board's adoption of that construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on reweighing evidence on appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit will not reweigh evidence or substitute its credibility determinations for the Board’s if substantial evidence supports the Board's conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deference to the Board's factfinding and credibility assessments means appellate counsel should focus on demonstrating a lack of substantial evidence rather than re-arguing the weight of the same evidence. Citations: Yorkey v. Diab, Velander v. Garner.
